summary: The central hypothesis — that crossover yield advantage predicts whether NSGA-II outperforms random search — is REFUTED. Llama at rate=50 has the highest yield advantage (14.74x) of any condition, yet was predicted to have the lowest (<3x). The negative NSGA-II gap for Llama at rate=50 from iteration 7 appears to be a population-size artifact rather than a structural phenomenon.
key_points: Main hypothesis refuted: All four conditions show yield advantage >9x (range 9.7x–16.8x), making yield advantage useless as a gap-direction predictor. Llama rate=50 at 14.74x was predicted to be <3x — completely wrong direction.

Ablation reveals the real finding: With pop_size=40 (vs likely pop_size=20 in iter-7), NSGA-II wins for BOTH models at rate=50 (Qwen +55.4, Llama +38.6). Iter-7's Llama negative gap (-22.9) was likely an algorithmic artifact of insufficient population diversity, not a structural property of the search landscape.

Pareto fronts at rate=50 show 100% block_size=32 concentration for both models (even more extreme than rate=100's 93.5%), making crossover yield uniformly high and eliminating any model/rate differentiation the theory depended on.

Null model control partially confirmed: observed yield is ~3x above null baseline (~75% vs ~22%), confirming Pareto spatial structure exists, but the null baseline is 3–5x density (not ≈1x as predicted), indicating intrinsic topological bias in the crossover operator inflates baselines.

Exhaustive sweep densities matched predictions exactly (Qwen 4.50%, Llama 5.33%), validating the simulation infrastructure, but the per-axis KV NDR direction was wrong (Llama higher than Qwen, not lower).
